title: Chicken Adobo
subtitle: filipino chicken adobo
excerpt: Chicken adobo is a Filipino braise of chicken thighs cooked in vinegar, soy sauce, and garlic until the sauce reduces to a sticky glaze. It is the most widely eaten dish in the Philippines. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Adobo refers to the Filipino method of braising meat in vinegar and soy sauce. Every family has their own version. Some use coconut milk, some add potatoes, and the ratio of vinegar to soy varies widely.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch easily. Adobo keeps for 5 days in the fridge and its flavour improves overnight.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Adobo tastes better made a day ahead. Reheat in the pan and allow the sauce to re-glaze the chicken.

glossaryTerms.definition: The Filipino method of braising meat in vinegar, soy sauce, and garlic. The word comes from the Spanish adobar, meaning to marinate.
A pungent fermented condiment made from fish and salt. Added as an optional extra layer of umami in chicken adobo.

content.text: is one of the simplest braises you can make. The vinegar and soy sauce do all the work of seasoning and tenderising. The sauce reduces in the final stage to coat the chicken in a dark, glossy glaze. Serves 4.

content.text: Heat the oil in a dutch oven over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken pieces skin-side down for 4 to 5 minutes until deep golden. Turn and brown the other side for 2 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Pour off most of the fat. Add the garlic to the pot and cook for 1 minute until lightly golden.
Add the soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, dried chilli if using, and water. Add 3 bay leaves if you have them. Stir to combine.
Return the chicken to the pot. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook for 25 minutes.
Remove the lid. Increase the heat to medium-high. Cook for a further 8 to 10 minutes until the sauce reduces to a glaze and coats the chicken. Turn the pieces once during this stage.
Add a splash of fish sauce if using. Serve over steamed white rice.

attrs.solution: Filipino adobo is supposed to be tangy. If it is overwhelming, add a pinch more sugar. The ratio of vinegar to soy can be adjusted to taste in future batches.
Cook uncovered over higher heat. The sauce reduces by about half. It should coat the back of a spoon before you stop.

attrs.problem: The chicken skin is not crisp.
attrs.solution: Transfer the cooked chicken to a hot frying pan skin-side down for 2 to 3 minutes at the end to crisp the skin separately.

content.text: Chicken adobo is considered the national dish of the Philippines. It is eaten in every household across the country, with each family keeping their own version. Some add coconut milk, some use pork, and some leave out the soy entirely. The vinegar was originally used as a preservative in the tropical heat before refrigeration.
